# House Price Prediction — SkillCraft ML Task 01

## Overview

This repository is an educational linear-regression exercise. It generates a **synthetic housing-style dataset**, compares a mean-value baseline with a linear regression model, evaluates them on the same held-out test set, accepts one user-entered example, and plots test-set predictions.

**Important limitation:** the program does not use real housing sales data. Its target is generated by a formula in the code, so its output is a synthetic target value—not a real house-price estimate. Do not use it for real-estate, financial, or other real-world decisions.

## What it demonstrates

- Generating reproducible sample data with NumPy.
- Organizing features and targets with pandas.
- Splitting data into training and test sets.
- Comparing a DummyRegressor mean baseline with scikit-learn LinearRegression.
- Evaluating held-out predictions with MAE, RMSE, and R-squared.
- Validating interactive numeric input.
- Plotting actual versus predicted synthetic target values for the test set.

## Measured result on the synthetic benchmark

With the default random seed (42), **500 generated rows**, and an 80/20 train/test split, both models are fitted using the same 400 training rows and evaluated on the same 100 held-out rows.

| Model | Test MAE | Test RMSE | Test R² |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Mean-value baseline | 4.501 | 5.615 | -0.001 |
| Linear Regression | 1.490 | 1.907 | 0.885 |

Compared with the mean-value baseline on this fixed synthetic test split, Linear Regression reduced MAE by **66.89%** and RMSE by **66.04%**.

These results are reproducible for the code and seed above but apply **only to the formula-generated synthetic target**. They are not model accuracy on real homes, and they must not be described as real-estate valuation performance.

## Features used

| Feature | Meaning in this demonstration |
| --- | --- |
| rm | Average number of rooms |
| lstat | Lower-status population percentage |
| tax | Property-tax feature |
| target | Synthetic value generated from a formula plus random noise |

The synthetic target formula is:

    target = 5 * rooms - 0.5 * status - 0.01 * tax + random_noise

The feature names are inspired by common housing-dataset terminology, but this project does not load the Boston Housing dataset or any real-world dataset.

## Requirements

- Python 3.10 or later
- NumPy
- pandas
- scikit-learn
- Matplotlib

Install the dependencies:

    python -m pip install numpy pandas scikit-learn matplotlib

## Run the program

From the repository directory:

    python SCT_01.py

The program prints the baseline and linear regression results, prompts for three feature values, and opens a plot of test-set predictions.

## How evaluation works

The data is split into training and test sets (80% / 20%). The mean baseline predicts the average target value from the training set for every test row. Linear Regression fits the three generated input features using the same training rows. MAE, RMSE, and R² are then computed on the same held-out test set.

The metrics only indicate how well the model fits this generated example. They are **not evidence of performance on real housing data**.

## Known limitations and possible next steps

- Replace the synthetic data with a suitable, properly licensed real dataset for a real predictive-modelling experiment.
- Add cross-validation and compare model performance across multiple splits.
- Examine residuals and feature assumptions.
- Document the dataset source, units, and limitations if real data is introduced.
- Do not present this educational demo as a production house-price prediction system.
